comments.comment: 5:40 intuitive understanding over mathematical measurement = freeer feeling   8:30 reference every stroke to be a guideline fir perspective instead of needing a perfect mathematically correct vanishing point lines  Always think when you draw something, where is the upper &lower VP?  Where is the left and right VP? And from there try to FIRST draw the parts in the subject that can indicate those VP For Kim frog helmet he started with the front side if helmet which indicated right VP then the right side of helmet slightly indicated left side VP The toad eyes on helmet (when thinking about the square than hold sit inside) will tell where the upper VP is  Then the glasses give a reinforcement of where the right and left VP are   6:35 also can use contour lines to indicate form but also help reinforce VP for yourself throughout the drawing   9:30 once you are always thinking about objects as where they are in perspective/ “mastering the cube” Then you will improve very fast

comments.comment: 5:33 I have a question for you Stan, I think I have heard you mentioning "the math behind perspective", but I saw Marshall's videos, I've read enough of perspective books to understand the basic concepts like vanishing points, horizon line, etc. but I've never seen math used beyond the basic concepts of perpendicular, parallel, oblique and at most angle measurements. Is that all there is? or is there a point where you really get deep into trigonometry?  In computer graphics you have a view matrix, a projection matrix and a model matrix that map 3d coordinates to 2d coordinates in the projection plane, I understand enough of it to look deeper and find how it could be done on paper, there's a lot of sine and cosine calculations, angles to radians, vectors, matrices and even quaternions, which I get, but I still feel like I am missing the glue between human drawing and computer drawing, and "the math behind perspective drawing" just seems to be it, yet I am not able to find math past elementary school math in perspective drawing, just a lot of intuition. Thank you and best regards!

comments.comment: What he says at 15:12 is KEY for anyone wanting to draw or paint more loosely and fluidly. He basically says that he used to draw very tightly and meticulously. Repetition of this technique is what led to an intuitive understanding of form until he no longer needed to have an iron grip on what he was drawing. The understanding was inside him so he could draw the lines as quickly and fluidly as he felt like and it would still turn out looking correct. If you feel like you draw too “tight” just keep practicing over and over and really try to internalize the form, without thinking too much about the tightness or looseness. Before you can draw loosely you draw tightly, even a savant like Kim Jung Gi.
